Communication was by telephone and telegraph; no mobile or digital devices

crime_subtype: planted evidence to implicate a rival

surface_summary: Benjamin H. Kyle was found murdered in the Bliss Museum with a heavy statue nearby and a rare scarab pin beside him, implicating Dr. Bliss. The evidence seemed to point to Bliss, who was arrested, but inconsistencies and a death trap suggested a more complex plot involving other household members.
accepted_facts: Benjamin H. Kyle was murdered by a blow to the head with a statue of Sakhmet
Dr. Bliss’s scarab pin and a financial report were found near the body
Bliss was found with his fingerprints on the statue and had bloody footprints leading to his study
An opium powder was found in Bliss’s coffee, suggesting he was drugged
inferred_conclusions: Dr. Bliss was the murderer acting alone
The bloody footprints and planted evidence conclusively prove Bliss’s guilt
The death trap was intended to kill Kyle and implicate Salveter
mechanism_description: Dr. Bliss murdered Benjamin H. Kyle by striking him from behind with a heavy mace, then arranged the scene by placing the statue of Sakhmet as a death trap and planting his own scarab pin and financial report near the body to implicate himself. He drugged his coffee with opium to create an alibi. Later, Anûpu Hani killed Bliss to end the plot, carefully avoiding leaving evidence.
delivery_path: Bliss arranged an appointment with Kyle and ensured Kyle would come early to inspect new artifacts
Bliss drugged his own coffee with opium to simulate being asleep
Bliss killed Kyle by a blow from behind using a mace, then placed the statue of Sakhmet to simulate a death trap
Bliss planted his scarab pin and financial report near Kyle’s body and made bloody footprints with one tennis shoe
Bliss attempted to frame Salveter by planting forged letters and hiding the dagger sheath in Salveter’s room
Scarlett discovered the plot and was attacked and hidden in a sarcophagus by Bliss
Anûpu Hani, knowing the truth and to protect the innocent, killed Bliss by breaking the statue of Anûbis over his head
outcome_result: Dr. Bliss was the murderer of Benjamin H. Kyle, and Anûpu Hani killed Bliss to end the plot; the case was solved by Philo Vance.

false_assumption.statement: Dr. Bliss was the sole murderer and acted without any accomplices or interference.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: All direct evidence such as fingerprints, footprints, and planted items pointed to Bliss, and he was found with incriminating items and attempted escape. The opium in his coffee suggested he was drugged and innocent.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It conceals the involvement of Anûpu Hani who ultimately killed Bliss, and the fact that Bliss’s evidence was deliberately planted to implicate himself and frame Salveter.

supporting_points: Bliss’s fingerprints on the statue of Sakhmet
The scarab pin belonging to Bliss found beside the victim
Financial report in the victim’s hand prepared by Bliss
Bloody footprints matching Bliss’s tennis shoe found at the scene
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The evidence was deliberately planted by Bliss to mislead investigators and frame Salveter; Bliss had an alibi supported by the opium in his coffee and was ultimately killed by Hani.

red_herrings.description: Hani’s talk of the vengeance of Sakhmet and mystical retribution suggested he might be involved in a supernatural killing or be the murderer.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Hani used superstition as a cover to protect Salveter and Meryt-Amen and to mislead investigators.

red_herrings.description: Salveter’s hieroglyphic letter containing ominous words suggested he had a motive and was involved in the murder.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The letter was a linguistic exercise and was forged and planted by Bliss to implicate Salveter.

closed_circle.rationale: The suspects are limited to the household and close associates with access to the museum and house during the time of the murder; no outside intruders were possible due to locked doors and lack of evidence.

time_windows: Kyle’s arrival and murder between 10:00 and 10:30 a.m.
Salveter’s absence from 9:30 p.m. Saturday to next morning
Scarlett’s attack between 8:00 and 8:30 p.m. Saturday

inference_path.correction: Pin was planted to implicate Bliss
inference_path.effect: Bliss’s guilt is not proven by pin alone

inference_path.correction: Bliss handled statue earlier to straighten it, not to kill

inference_path.correction: Only one tennis shoe found downstairs; other shoe hidden upstairs

Butler’s testimony on locked front door

inference_path.correction: Letter was planted by Bliss to frame Salveter

inference_path.correction: Hani killed Bliss to end the murderous plot
inference_path.effect: Bliss’s death was murder by Hani

discriminating_test.design: Vance reconstructed the death trap by placing the statue of Sakhmet precariously balanced on a pencil wedge on the cabinet edge with the curtain partially drawn and the loose brass ring under the statue’s base. Pulling the curtain caused the statue to topple exactly where Kyle’s head had been, demonstrating the plausibility of the staged death trap.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The test showed that the statue could fall and kill someone standing in front of the cabinet, supporting the theory that the trap was staged after the murder to mislead investigators.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The statue must topple and land precisely on the spot corresponding to Kyle’s head position, confirming the trap’s feasibility.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed descriptions of the physical evidence, the timing of arrivals and departures, and the relationships and motives of the household members. The planted evidence and the forged letter are clearly presented, as are the inconsistencies in Bliss’s alibi and the presence of opium. The death trap experiment is described in detail, allowing the reader to question the obvious conclusions. The final confession and unmasking are foreshadowed, making the solution accessible to a careful and attentive reader.
